examples.problem_statement: Find sets of direction numbers for the direction cosines [2/3, -2/3, -1/3].

solution.description: Multiply each of the three direction cosines 2/3, -2/3 and -1/3 by 3 to clear the common denominator, which leaves the whole-number triple 2, -2, -1. Any nonzero multiple of that triple, such as 4, -4, -2 or -2, 2, 1, names the same direction, so there are infinitely many correct answers.

examples.problem_statement: Find direction numbers for the line through points P1(x1, y1, z1) and P2(x2, y2, z2).

solution.description: With no numbers given, work from the two points directly: subtract the coordinates of P1 from those of P2 one axis at a time, so the differences x2 - x1, y2 - y1 and z2 - z1 record how far the line travels along each axis. Subtracting in the other order gives the opposite triple, which describes the same line traversed backwards.

examples.problem_statement: Find a set of direction numbers for direction cosines [1/2, 1/sqrt(2), -1/2].

solution.description: Multiply each cosine 1/2, 1/sqrt(2) and -1/2 by 2 to clear the denominator 2, giving 1, sqrt(2), -1. Scaling only removes the common denominator; it does not have to make every entry an integer, so the middle entry stays irrational.

concept.technique_name: substitution method for a linear-quadratic system

solution.description: Of the two equations only 5x + y = 7 is linear, so it is the cheap one to rearrange: isolating y gives y = 7 - 5x, an expression that can stand in for y everywhere else.
Put 7 - 5x in place of y in 4x squared + 3y squared = 16. The system in two unknowns becomes a single equation in x alone, which is the whole point of substituting.
Expand the squared binomial (7 - 5x) squared as 49 - 70x + 25x squared, keeping the middle term negative because the binomial is a difference.
Multiply each term inside the bracket by the 3 in front of it, so 3 times 49 - 70x + 25x squared becomes 147 - 210x + 75x squared.
Collect the two x squared terms, 4x squared and 75x squared, into 79x squared, so the left side reads 79x squared - 210x + 147.
Move the 16 across by subtracting it from both sides. The equation 79x squared - 210x + 131 = 0 is now in the standard form the quadratic formula expects.
With a = 79, b = -210 and c = 131, apply the quadratic formula rather than hunting for factors of an awkward trinomial with a prime leading coefficient.
Evaluate the discriminant b squared - 4ac as 44100 - 41396 = 2704. Since 2704 is 52 squared, the square root is exact and both roots will be rational.
Substitute the square root 52 back into the formula, so the two roots are (210 + 52)/158 and (210 - 52)/158.
Carry out the two divisions: 262/158 reduces to 131/79, and 158/158 is exactly 1. These are the two x values of the system.
Each x needs its own partner, so send both values back through y = 7 - 5x. From x = 1 comes y = 2, and from x = 131/79 comes y = -102/79.

examples.answer: The solutions are $x = 1, y = 2$ and $x = \frac{131}{79}, y = -\frac{102}{79}$.

solution.description: Equation (38.1) carries 9y squared and (38.2) carries -2y squared, so the y squared terms will only cancel once their sizes match. Multiplying (38.1) through by 2 raises its y squared coefficient to 18, which is half of the matching job.
Multiply (38.2) by 9 so its y squared coefficient becomes -18, exactly the opposite of the 18 produced in the previous step. The two equations are now primed to cancel on addition.
Add the two scaled equations term by term. On the left 18y squared and -18y squared destroy each other, and on the right 144 and 171 combine.
What survives is 35x squared = 315, so x squared = 9 and x is 3 or -3. Both signs are kept, because squaring hides the sign of x.
Send x = 3 back into the original (38.1): 4 times 9 is 36, leaving 9y squared = 36, so y squared = 4 and y is 2 or -2.
Repeat with x = -3. Since x appears only as x squared, the arithmetic is identical and again yields y = 2 or -2, so all four sign combinations are genuine solutions.

concept.technique_name: factoring a homogeneous quadratic to split a system into cases

solution.description: Equation (38.3) is set equal to zero and every term has degree two, which is exactly the shape that factors cleanly: x squared - 3xy + 2y squared becomes (x - y)(x - 2y).
A product can only be zero when one of its factors is zero, so the single equation splits into two simple relations, x - y = 0 and x - 2y = 0, that is x = y or x = 2y.

solution.operation: Case 1: Substitute x = y into second equation
solution.description: Take the first branch, x = y, and carry it into (38.4). Replacing every y by x turns 2x squared + 3xy - y squared into 2x squared + 3x squared - x squared, which collapses to 4x squared = 13.

solution.operation: Solve for x and y in Case 1
solution.description: Divide by 4 and take the square root, giving x = sqrt(13)/2 or its negative. Because this branch assumed y = x, y takes the same value and the same sign as x.

solution.operation: Case 2: Substitute x = 2y into second equation
solution.description: Now the second branch, x = 2y, goes into (38.4). The terms become 8y squared + 6y squared - y squared, which adds to 13y squared, and that equals 13.

solution.operation: Solve for y and x in Case 2
solution.description: So y squared = 1 and y is 1 or -1. Feeding each back through x = 2y gives x = 2 or -2, with the sign of x locked to the sign of y.
Collect the two pairs from each branch into the four solutions, keeping the signs matched within every pair. A mixed pair such as (2, -1) would fail the first equation.

examples.answer: The solutions are $x = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}, y = \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}$; $x = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}, y = -\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}$; $x = 2, y = 1$; $x = -2, y = -1$

solution.operation: Recognize that the variable appears in the exponent, so logarithms are needed.
solution.description: The unknown sits in the exponent of 2 to the x, where ordinary algebra cannot reach it. Taking the logarithm of both sides is the move that brings an exponent down to ground level, and any consistent base works.

solution.operation: Take common logarithm (base 10) of both sides.
solution.description: Apply the base-10 logarithm to each side, so 2 to the x = 7 becomes log of 2 to the x equals log 7. Applying the same function to two equal quantities keeps them equal.

solution.operation: Apply the power rule of logarithms.
solution.description: The power rule lets the exponent step out in front of the logarithm, so log of 2 to the x becomes x times log 2. The equation is now linear in x.

solution.operation: Isolate x by dividing both sides by log 2.
solution.description: Since x is multiplied by log 2, divide both sides by log 2 to leave x alone as the ratio of log 7 to log 2.

solution.operation: Compute the numerical values using a calculator or log table.
solution.description: Look up or key in the two common logarithms needed for that ratio: log 7 is about 0.8451 and log 2 is about 0.3010.
Divide 0.8451 by 0.3010 to turn the ratio into the number 2.808, the approximate value of x.

solution.operation: Verify by substituting back into the original equation.
solution.description: Check the answer by raising 2 to the power 2.808, which comes out near 7.0. The small gap is only the rounding carried in the two logarithm values.
